subtitle: Whether staff are in the office, at home or both, you can help them participate, use shared information and complete their work. This course focuses on accessibility across in-person and remote settings.
scope: For DHS supervisors and team leads coordinating hybrid or remote work. The course supports accessible work practices and proper accommodation referrals. It does not establish telework eligibility, change attendance or labor rules, authorize equipment purchases or replace an individual accommodation decision.
introTranscript: Hybrid work is more than a camera in a room. People need to hear the discussion, follow the information, join the conversation and complete the work afterward. Follow a team through planning, a hybrid discussion and shared work. Practice removing barriers while keeping accommodation requests, employment rules and technology decisions with the people responsible for them. No one needs to share personal medical information with the group.

lessons.title: Map participation and work across locations
lessons.summary: The team’s task can depend on the room, platform, materials and follow-up. Review the complete work experience.
lessons.objective: Identify access points in a hybrid work task beyond the video connection.
objectives: Identify access points in a hybrid work task beyond the video connection.
Distinguish an observable participation barrier from an assumption about effort.
Map relevant owners without changing agency telework or attendance rules.
takeaways: A connection does not prove effective participation.
Look at the task across room, platform and materials.
Ask about the barrier without guessing a diagnosis or motive.
lessons.statement: Someone can be connected and still be unable to hear, understand, contribute or finish the task.

image.caption: A hybrid task crosses the room and the remote interface; both need attention.

intro.heading: Follow the task rather than the attendance label
intro.body:
A DHS team holds a hybrid planning meeting. Remote staff join successfully, but they cannot hear comments from the far end of the room. A chart is visible only on a wall, and the final decision is made after the online portion ends. The attendance record shows everyone present. That does not establish that everyone could participate in the work. Map the task: receive the information, follow discussion, contribute, understand the decision and complete the assigned action.

Barriers can occur in different parts of that path. The room may have poor microphone coverage; the digital materials may lack usable structure; the platform’s controls may not support a participant’s method of interaction. A meeting practice may privilege the room by accepting only spoken interruptions or side conversations. Do not assume one technology feature resolves every issue.

MNIT’s guidance asks organizers to consider accessibility in planning and use presentation practices that support participation. The state digital standard also concerns relevant internal information and tools, not only public websites. These responsibilities are distinct from the agency’s actual telework, attendance, security and employment rules. This course does not change where a person is authorized to work or promise that any location or equipment request will be approved.

Begin with an observable description: which information or action was unavailable, in which task and under what conditions. “The room comments were not audible to remote participants” gives the owner something to address. “Remote staff are disengaged” turns an unexamined barrier into a judgment about people. Ask practical questions and arrange the proper review.

For the course exercise, use a practice task and identify the room host, facilitator, material owner, technology support and follow-up owner through actual agency roles. A person’s current accommodation need belongs in its appropriate confidential process alongside these shared improvements.

inThisLesson: Separate access planning from telework authority.
lessons.keyStatement: Presence is not the same as effective access to the work.

flashcards.back: The steps from receiving information to contributing and acting on a decision. A successful sign-in is only one part.
A task-specific fact, such as inaudible room comments or an unreachable control. It supports inquiry without diagnosing the person or guessing effort.
A practice designed for the group, such as usable materials and clear turn-taking. It can reduce barriers but does not replace individual accommodation.
The agency-approved location, attendance and related employment arrangement. A course practice does not change it or delegate approval authority.

items.title: The information
items.body: Can people receive the material in a usable form, not only as a small image on a shared screen? Identify documents, charts and instructions before assuming the meeting tool will carry all the meaning.

items.title: The conversation
items.body: Can people hear the speakers and enter the discussion? A good connection cannot fix a speaker too far from the microphone or a decision made in an unshared side conversation. Assign facilitation and technical support deliberately.

items.title: The next action
items.body: Do people receive the final decision and clear responsibilities afterward? A meeting can seem inclusive while its follow-up leaves remote staff without the information needed to act. Check this stage as part of the same task.

tabs.heading: Describe the issue at the right level

tabs.label: Task fact
tabs.body: “The wall chart’s values were not included in the shared file.” This identifies information missing from the remote path and can guide an accessible correction.

tabs.label: Unexamined judgment
tabs.body: “The remote staff did not care.” Silence does not establish motive. First check the available information, contribution route and actual task conditions.

tabs.label: Process question
tabs.body: “Who can approve a requested individual work adjustment?” Route it through the authorized accommodation or employment process. The group’s meeting plan does not decide it.

check.question: Everyone joined the hybrid call, but remote participants could not hear room discussion. What can the leader accurately conclude?
check.correct: The connection worked, but the discussion path had an access barrier that needs investigation and response.
wrong: All participants had effective access because attendance was recorded.
Remote staff must have chosen not to participate.
This course automatically authorizes any requested telework change.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Separate the observed connection from the unavailable discussion. Identify the room and facilitation response without making unsupported judgments or changing employment authority.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Attendance is limited evidence. Look at the actual information and task before judging engagement; accommodation and work arrangements still use their proper processes.

items.text: Remote participants could not hear the far-end room speaker.
Assign a facilitator to check the remote contribution route.
Silence proves the remote staff were uninterested.
The required chart was not in the distributed material.
Identify an owner for accessible follow-up decisions.
Successful sign-in proves every part of the meeting was accessible.

lessons.next: Next, prepare the materials, room and request route before the meeting starts.

scenario.context: In this example, a team lead notices that remote colleagues rarely interrupt a lively room discussion. The lead wants to lower their participation rating without checking whether they can hear or enter the discussion.
options: Assume location explains lack of effort.
Examine the information and contribution path, address observed barriers and keep formal performance decisions in their appropriate process.
Make all personal accommodation information public to explain attendance.
responses: Location and silence do not establish effort. The actual conditions need inquiry.
This identifies what can be observed and improved without deciding a performance question from an incomplete impression.
Personal medical or accommodation information is not needed for a group access discussion. Preserve confidentiality.

lessons.transfer: Map a practice hybrid task from information to action. Name one room risk, one digital risk and the responsible next question.

move.control: You can examine the complete task before judging participation.
move.failure: Connection or location is used as a shortcut for access or effort.
move.next: Describe the actual barrier and assign the appropriate shared and individual response routes.

lessons.title: Prepare a usable meeting before people arrive
lessons.summary: Advance materials, clear access information and checked settings reduce preventable barriers without requiring personal disclosure.
lessons.objective: Prepare an invitation with useful access information and a real request route.
objectives: Prepare an invitation with useful access information and a real request route.
Identify materials and room or platform settings to check in advance.
Respond to a late access question without treating a planning deadline as automatic denial.
takeaways: Share necessary material in a usable form.
Explain the provided access features and request contact.
Planning dates help preparation; individual requests still need the appropriate response.
lessons.statement: Good preparation lets people focus on the work rather than finding a way into it.

image.caption: A usable agenda and materials support preparation across different ways of reading and participating.

intro.heading: Create a clear starting point
intro.body:
The DHS team sends an invitation saying only “Join the meeting.” It includes no agenda, materials or contact for an access question. A participant may need to prepare with an accessible file, arrange an individual adjustment or understand how a provided service will work. The organizer can make that information clear without asking everyone to list disabilities.

MNIT’s meeting guidance recommends stating the accommodations being provided and giving a contact and planning date for additional requests. Ask about the needed service, not the disability. For an employee’s disability-related request, use the agency accommodation process and appropriate coordinator. A planning date helps arrange support but should not be described as a universal legal cutoff that automatically permits rejection of a later request. Respond and involve the responsible process.

Prepare the necessary documents in a usable format and share them through the approved route. A slide image projected in a room may not allow someone to navigate its content independently. A structured document can support review in advance and during the meeting. Consider the specific material, required interaction and confidentiality rules; this course does not authorize distributing private records simply to improve convenience.

Check practical conditions with the appropriate support staff. Can the room’s microphones capture speakers? Can remote participants access the information and contribution channel? Can provided captioning or interpretation be seen and used under the planned arrangement? Platform features and agency configurations change, so avoid relying on an old instruction that a particular button always works the same way.

For important unfamiliar arrangements, a short supported rehearsal can reveal missing setup or instructions. It is not a complete technical audit or a guarantee for every participant. Record what was checked and what remains unresolved. A host, material owner and support contact make the plan more reliable than expecting a participant to solve each problem once the meeting begins.

inThisLesson: Provide usable materials through approved channels.
Check the room and planned services.
lessons.keyStatement: Preparation can reduce barriers without demanding a personal explanation from every participant.

flashcards.back: Practical information about provided services, material availability and how to raise a need. It should be understandable and tied to a real contact.
A date helping the organizer prepare services. Do not portray it as automatic authority to deny a later individual accommodation request.
Information that can be read and navigated appropriately for its purpose. A picture of a document is not automatically equivalent to its structured source.
A focused check of the planned arrangement. It can reveal issues but does not prove complete conformance or every person’s effective access.

accordion.heading: Prepare the parts people depend on

items.title: Invitation and contact
items.body: Say what is provided and how a person can ask about another need. Use the actual responsible contact, not an invented office. A vague statement that accessibility matters is less useful than clear next steps.

items.title: Material and timing
items.body: Share relevant usable content early enough to support preparation where feasible. Keep it current and use approved distribution. If material changes during the meeting, make the meaningful change available rather than assuming everyone can see the screen.

items.title: Room and technology
items.body: Work with appropriate staff to check audio, controls and planned access services. A hybrid arrangement can require support for both locations. Record an unresolved item and its owner instead of waiting for a participant to discover it.

tabs.label: Routine plan
tabs.body: Use maintained templates, clear materials and an access contact. Routine practices reduce repeated barriers while leaving room for a person’s specific request.

tabs.label: Unfamiliar setup
tabs.body: Arrange a focused check with support staff and relevant participants where appropriate. Record the actual setup and limits; a vendor feature list does not establish the configured experience.

tabs.label: Late request
tabs.body: Listen, clarify the needed service and involve the appropriate process promptly. A missed planning date is not by itself the full decision about a disability-related request. Avoid promising a result beyond your authority.

check.question: An employee asks about an access service after the invitation’s planning date. What should the organizer do?
check.correct: Respond promptly, clarify the needed service and involve the appropriate agency process rather than automatically denying it because of the date.
wrong: Deny every later request without discussion.
Ask for the employee’s complete medical records in the group email.
Guarantee approval of every requested service personally.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The date supports planning, while the actual request still needs a proper response. Ask about the service and keep documentation and decisions with the appropriate roles.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A planning date does not replace the process. Avoid improper medical requests and unsupported promises; respond to the need and use the responsible route.

sorting.heading: What does the preparation note do?

items.text: The invitation identifies the actual access contact and provided services.
The host checks microphone coverage with support staff.
A disability-related employee request is forwarded promptly through the accommodation route.
A late need receives a response rather than automatic rejection.
Every participant must send a diagnosis to receive the agenda.
An old platform instruction proves today’s configuration works.

lessons.next: Next, make the live discussion usable for people in the room and online.

scenario.context: In this example, a team lead shares only a screenshot of a complex agenda and says anyone needing another format should announce their disability at the meeting.
options: Use a structured accessible agenda, provide a private practical request route and review the current material before distribution.
Retain the screenshot because everyone can zoom.
Post medical questions in the meeting chat.
responses: This improves the shared starting point and respects individual privacy. Enlargement alone does not preserve structure or answer every need.
Zoom does not turn an image into a navigable structured document. Examine the actual content.
The group does not need medical details. Use the appropriate confidential route for individual requests.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice invitation stating the purpose, material route, provided access information and real role responsible for other requests.

move.control: You can make the starting information clear.
move.failure: The meeting begins with preventable barriers and public disclosure pressure.
move.next: Prepare usable material and a private request route, and verify the planned arrangement.

lessons.title: Facilitate one discussion across two spaces
lessons.summary: Turn-taking, shared meaning and a supported contribution route help prevent the room from becoming the only place decisions happen.
lessons.objective: Apply turn-taking and speaker-identification practices to a hybrid discussion.
objectives: Apply turn-taking and speaker-identification practices to a hybrid discussion.
Describe important visual information without claiming one script serves every access need.
Respond to a participation barrier during the meeting without exposing private information.
takeaways: Manage the discussion so both locations can contribute.
State the meaning of important visuals and actions.
Pause and respond when the planned access path fails.
lessons.statement: A hybrid discussion should have one shared decision path, even when participants use different ways to follow and contribute.

image.caption: A facilitator can keep the room conversation and remote contribution channel connected.

intro.heading: Make the discussion available in real time
intro.body:
The DHS team begins discussing a chart. Several people in the room talk at once while a remote colleague types a question. The facilitator moves on without seeing it. The problem is not solved by having a meeting link. Facilitation must connect the discussion, information and contribution paths. Assigning a person to monitor remote contributions can help; decide that role before the meeting rather than leaving it to chance.

MNIT recommends introductions, clear speaker identification, turn-taking and meaningful descriptions of visual information. Say the relevant comparison or action instead of “as you can see here.” When someone asks a question, repeat or summarize it so people who did not hear it can follow the answer. Pause deliberately for contributions rather than assuming immediate speech is the only signal of interest. These practices support participation but do not replace a needed individual service.

A room conversation that produces a decision after the remote meeting ends excludes that decision from the shared path. Keep the substantive decision in the accessible meeting or provide a properly arranged further discussion. A written follow-up can preserve an outcome, but does not automatically replace the opportunity to contribute before the decision.

If audio, captions, interpretation visibility or another needed path fails, acknowledge the barrier and use the appropriate response. Depending on the task and circumstances, that can involve a pause, technical support or a properly arranged continuation. Do not decide that one participant can simply catch up later without examining the actual access and agency responsibilities.

Keep personal information private. Explain the task adjustment without naming a diagnosis or a confidential accommodation. The group can hear “we need to restore the audio path before this decision” without hearing why a particular person needs it. Afterward, record the operational issue and responsible follow-up through the proper process so the next meeting does not repeat it.

inThisLesson: Connect remote questions to the discussion.
Respond when an access path fails.
lessons.keyStatement: The decision should be available through the same supported participation path as the discussion.

flashcards.back: Managing how the group receives information and contributes. It includes the room and remote routes rather than only choosing the next in-room speaker.
The information or action a visual supports. Saying the important finding is more useful than pointing to an unseen region or describing color alone.
The supported way a participant asks a question or offers input. The facilitator should know how it enters the shared discussion.
A failure in the path needed for participation. Respond to the task and relevant duty; do not expose private information or assume a later recording resolves everything.

items.title: Manage overlapping speech
items.body: Identify speakers and encourage one contribution at a time. This makes the discussion easier to follow and can support captioning or interpretation. Do not infer that rapid interruption is the best evidence of leadership or engagement.

items.title: Describe the relevant information
items.body: For a chart, state the measure, comparison and important finding with its limits. For a demonstration, explain the action being taken. A brief description should convey necessary meaning, while the accessible material provides detail.

items.title: Check the shared path
items.body: Before closing a decision, make sure remote contributions have been considered and the information is available. This is a suggested facilitation practice, not a guarantee that every formal decision rule is satisfied. Use the actual agency procedure when it applies.

tabs.label: Audio fails
tabs.body: State the observed problem and arrange support. Do not label someone inattentive for failing to respond to inaudible discussion. Determine the suitable pause or continuation with the relevant responsibilities in mind.

tabs.label: Visuals are unavailable
tabs.body: Provide the meaningful information through the supported route and usable material. Simply enlarging the room display does not help someone who cannot access it.

tabs.label: A private need is raised
tabs.body: Move personal accommodation details to the confidential process while addressing the immediate task appropriately. The group can understand a practical change without hearing medical information.

check.question: A substantive decision is made in a room side conversation after remote participants leave. What should the leader examine?
check.correct: Whether the decision and opportunity to contribute were available through the shared supported process, and what appropriate continuation or correction is needed.
wrong: Whether remote participants should have guessed that the room would continue.
Whether posting an unexplained outcome automatically fixes every participation issue.
Whether a participant’s diagnosis can be announced to justify repeating the discussion.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Keep the task and participation question central. A follow-up outcome may be useful, but it does not automatically replace a missed contribution opportunity or the actual decision procedure.
check.feedbackIncorrect: People outside the room should not have to guess that a decision discussion continued. Posting an unexplained outcome does not restore their missed opportunity to contribute or automatically satisfy the actual decision procedure. Announcing a diagnosis would expose medical information without resolving the participation problem. Examine the shared supported decision path and use the appropriate process for any continuation or correction.

items.text: Identify the speaker and repeat a question before answering.
State the important chart finding in words.
Pause the task to restore the required audio path.
Arrange the appropriate supported continuation when a service fails.
Make the final decision in an unshared room-only conversation.
Treat a remote typed question as less relevant because it was not spoken.

scenario.context: A practice remote participant says room discussion is inaudible during a decision. The facilitator proposes finishing anyway and telling that person to watch the same unclear recording later.
options: Acknowledge the barrier, arrange the appropriate technical or access response and determine a supported way to continue the decision.
Announce the participant’s confidential accommodation to the group.
responses: Attendance does not establish access. The actual task barrier still requires response.
This addresses the current participation problem without assuming the recording is an effective substitute. Use the actual agency obligations and decision process.
Private details are unnecessary. Explain the operational change and preserve confidentiality.

lessons.transfer: Draft a practice facilitation plan naming the turn-taking method, remote contribution owner, visual-description practice and response to an access interruption.

move.control: You can connect the discussion across locations.
move.failure: The room controls the information and final decision.
move.next: Keep the contribution path supported and respond to observed interruptions before assuming participation was effective.

lessons.title: Make shared work usable after the meeting
lessons.summary: Documents, recordings and collaboration tasks need accessible meaning and structure. Asynchronous work is not automatically accessible.
lessons.objective: Identify a shared document or collaboration activity that can block work after a meeting.
objectives: Identify a shared document or collaboration activity that can block work after a meeting.
Distinguish a recording from an accessible replacement for the task.
Plan a usable contribution alternative through the appropriate work process.
takeaways: Shared information needs usable structure and alternatives.
Recording a meeting does not automatically make it accessible.
An alternative method must preserve the relevant work purpose.
lessons.statement: People need to use the information and contribute to the work, not merely receive a link.

image.caption: The work continues in documents, comments and decisions that should remain understandable and navigable.

intro.heading: Review the next place the work happens
intro.body:
The DHS team finishes a useful meeting but posts its action list as an image and asks staff to add ideas by dragging sticky notes on a digital board. One staff member cannot operate that interaction with their input method. The meeting itself was only one part of the task. Shared documents, comments, boards and final decisions need attention too.

Minnesota’s digital standard applies to relevant internal tools and content. MNIT’s document guidance addresses structure, meaningful links, alternatives and contrast in final files. Use maintained authoring practices and review the version staff actually receive. A screen share or screenshot can be helpful in context, but should not be the only form of essential information when it does not provide usable access.

Recordings need their applicable media review. MNIT meeting guidance addresses transcripts for audio, captions for recorded material and meaningful access to important visuals. Automatic captions may misstate names, numbers or specialized terms. Review them and the other relevant requirements rather than assuming a recording feature guarantees access. Also follow the actual agency rules for recording, privacy, distribution and retention; this course does not authorize saving every discussion.

For a collaboration activity, identify the required outcome. If a board interaction is not usable, the work owner and appropriate support staff can examine a supported route for contributing the same necessary ideas. A proposed alternative should not silently remove the person from the decision or give them a lesser assignment. An individual accommodation question still uses its proper process, and a product barrier remains a product issue even when temporary support helps.

Give follow-up information a clear owner. State the decision, action, responsibility and where questions can be raised in a usable format. The course exercise uses practice material. Do not upload real recipient data or private staff details to an unapproved tool simply because it is easier to share.

inThisLesson: Review shared files and collaboration tasks.
Check recording access and agency permissions.
Preserve purpose in an alternative route.
Keep follow-up information clear and usable.
lessons.keyStatement: A link, recording or alternative is useful only when it supports the actual task and relevant requirements.

flashcards.back: Work completed outside the live meeting, such as reading, commenting or reviewing a document. Its digital content and actions still need access.
A route preserving the necessary information or contribution purpose. It is not merely any different activity or a weaker opportunity to participate.
Examining captions, transcripts and important visual information under applicable requirements, alongside the agency’s recording and distribution rules.
The responsible person who maintains usable decisions and action information through the actual work process. A meeting ending does not remove this responsibility.

items.title: Can people navigate the action list?
items.body: Use an appropriate structured file rather than an image-only list of necessary actions. Keep the order and ownership clear. Review the delivered version because export or conversion can change the structure.

items.title: Can people contribute meaningfully?
items.body: A digital board may require a gesture some people cannot use. Examine the required outcome and supported controls or alternatives. Do not assume the person is less creative because the selected interaction is difficult or inaccessible.

items.title: Can people use the recording?
items.body: Check the content and actual caption or transcript accuracy. Important visual actions may need an accessible explanation. A recording that repeats the original barrier is not a reliable substitute for the missed information or participation.

tabs.heading: Choose based on the work purpose

tabs.label: Reading information
tabs.body: Provide the necessary content in a usable form with meaningful structure and alternatives. A beautiful image may not preserve navigation or the information relationship.

tabs.label: Offering ideas
tabs.body: Preserve a meaningful contribution route through the work and, where needed, accommodation process. A temporary method should not automatically close the product issue or exclude the person from decisions.

tabs.label: Reviewing a recording
tabs.body: Follow authorized recording rules and relevant access requirements. Do not promise that a transcript alone addresses every video requirement or that a recording restores every missed live contribution opportunity.

check.question: A person cannot use a drag-only board to contribute required ideas. What should the team examine?
check.correct: The work purpose, the board’s supported controls and an effective contribution route through the appropriate process, while keeping the product barrier visible.
wrong: Whether the person should receive a less meaningful assignment.
Whether the person’s medical diagnosis should be posted on the board.
Whether any different activity automatically resolves all access responsibilities.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Focus on the actual outcome and a meaningful route. Shared tool review and individual accommodation can be related without being the same decision.
check.feedbackIncorrect: An alternative should preserve the necessary contribution, not remove the person from meaningful work. Avoid disclosure and unsupported claims that any workaround resolves everything.

items.text: Provide the action list in a structured accessible document.
Review specialized terms in the recording’s captions.
Examine supported board controls and a suitable input route.
Keep a person’s relevant ideas in the same decision process.
A recording link alone proves every media requirement is met.
Any temporary workaround permanently closes the product barrier.

scenario.context: In this example, a team publishes an image-only action list and tells a staff member to ask a coworker to read it whenever needed. The template is used every week.
options: Maintain the dependency indefinitely because one coworker is willing.
Make the action list a usable shared document, assign the template correction and address any current individual need through the appropriate process.
Remove the staff member from the weekly work.
responses: Temporary help may matter in a particular situation, but it does not automatically resolve the recurring digital barrier or applicable responsibilities.
This improves the common information path and preserves the proper response to the person’s present need. Verify the final file rather than only changing its appearance.
Exclusion does not preserve access to the work. Examine the information and responsibilities instead.

lessons.transfer: Review a practice follow-up file and collaboration task. Identify one shared repair and one question about preserving the actual contribution purpose.

move.control: You can maintain usable follow-up content.
move.failure: The meeting ends and inaccessible shared work is ignored.
move.next: Review the delivered documents, media and interaction route, with a responsible owner for the correction.

lessons.title: Respond to individual needs through the proper process
lessons.summary: Shared defaults help, but a disability-related request needs a prompt, confidential accommodation response.
lessons.objective: Recognize a request that may need the agency accommodation process.
objectives: Recognize a request that may need the agency accommodation process.
Explain the supervisor’s documentation boundary under MMB Policy 1433.
Distinguish a shared access improvement from an authorized individual work arrangement.
takeaways: A request can use ordinary words and different communication methods.
Supervisors must not request accommodation medical documentation.
Technology standards do not cancel separate employment accommodation duties.
lessons.statement: You can improve the group’s work and respond to an individual request without turning the conversation into a medical interview.

image.caption: A private task conversation should lead to the correct support and decision route.

intro.heading: Keep the need, roles and confidentiality clear
intro.body:
A DHS employee tells a supervisor, “Because of my condition, I need a different way to participate in the remote review.” That can be an accommodation request even without a form or the word ADA. MMB Policy 1433 recognizes requests communicated through different methods and does not require special terminology. Respond promptly and forward the request through the proper process, telling the requester who will handle the decision.

The supervisor can discuss the work duty, barrier and relevant outcome. Under the policy, supervisors and managers must not request medical information or documentation for accommodation. Appropriate documentation questions belong with the ADA Coordinator. Do not ask for a complete medical record, require the employee to explain the diagnosis to coworkers or turn the group meeting into the interactive process. Preserve the policy’s confidentiality boundaries.

Shared improvements may help the whole team: clearer materials, better audio or a maintained template. They do not automatically answer a specific request. The person’s participation, preference and actual effectiveness matter through the accommodation process. Nor does a requested work location or tool become automatically approved because a course example uses it. Actual duties, policies, authority and the individual circumstances must be considered by the responsible roles.

The state digital standard’s alternate-location provision is sometimes misunderstood. It does not itself obligate an agency to provide separate physical access or assistive equipment for home use, while it explicitly keeps employment accommodation obligations under separate rules. Do not use that statement as a blanket denial of an employee’s request. Route the specific need to the appropriate process.

Explain practical arrangements to coworkers only as needed for work, without revealing confidential medical or accommodation details. If a shared barrier needs technical repair, describe the task and product facts separately. Keeping the two paths distinct protects privacy and prevents a temporary individual adjustment from being mistaken for complete repair of the team’s tools.

inThisLesson: Forward promptly through the actual process.
Distinguish shared improvements from individual decisions.
lessons.keyStatement: Discuss the work and route the request; do not collect accommodation medical documentation yourself.

flashcards.back: A communication asking for a disability-related work adjustment without special legal terms. Recognize the possible request and use the actual process.
Discuss relevant work, forward the request and support implementation through the policy. Do not request accommodation medical documentation.
The appropriate ADA Coordinator handles documentation questions and related process responsibilities under the policy. Do not invent a separate local medical-review route.
The digital standard and employment accommodation process address related but distinct questions. A provision in one does not automatically decide every duty in the other.

items.title: Ask about the work barrier
items.body: Understand the duty and what prevents effective participation. The coordinator can address documentation questions when appropriate. You can have a useful task discussion without asking the employee to prove or describe a diagnosis to you.

items.title: Do not promise the outcome
items.body: Acknowledge the request and explain the actual next route. Avoid saying every preferred location or tool is approved, and avoid rejecting it from a general assumption. The responsible process considers the circumstances.

items.title: Communicate without disclosure
items.body: The team may need to know the meeting method or work arrangement. It does not need the confidential reason. Explain operational instructions and keep personal records in the authorized process.

tabs.label: Shared improvement
tabs.body: The team repairs room audio or a document template. This can reduce common barriers, but is not automatically an individual accommodation decision.

tabs.label: Individual request
tabs.body: The employee raises a disability-related need. Use the prompt confidential accommodation process and appropriate roles, even when a shared improvement is also underway.

tabs.label: Employment rule question
tabs.body: Attendance, telework eligibility and other employment rules have actual agency authority. An access learning exercise does not amend them or authorize a unilateral exception.

check.question: May a supervisor request an employee’s medical documentation to decide a hybrid-work accommodation under MMB Policy 1433?
check.correct: No. The supervisor discusses relevant work and routes the request; appropriate medical-documentation questions belong with the ADA Coordinator.
wrong: Yes, if the supervisor promises to keep every record in a personal folder.
Yes, because remote work removes confidentiality requirements.
No request counts unless the employee uses the exact legal term.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Keep the documentation boundary clear. A request can use ordinary language, and the supervisor can support the work discussion without collecting medical evidence.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Informal storage or work location does not change the policy. Recognize the request and use the appropriate roles rather than imposing special wording or collecting documentation.

items.text: Repair the room microphone and review the shared agenda.
Forward a disability-related request promptly through the policy.
Request the employee’s full medical file for the supervisor’s review.
Maintain usable templates for the group.
Consult the coordinator about appropriate documentation questions.
Announce confidential accommodation reasons to coworkers.

lessons.next: The final lesson follows both shared improvements and approved arrangements into actual effectiveness.

scenario.context: In this example, an employee requests a disability-related adjustment for remote work. The supervisor cites the digital standard’s alternate-location provision and denies the request without routing it.
options: Treat that provision as a blanket denial of every home-related request.
Ask coworkers to vote on the employee’s diagnosis.
Use the actual accommodation process; the digital standard’s provision does not cancel separate employment accommodation duties.
responses: The standard distinguishes its own obligation from separate accommodation rules. A specific request needs the appropriate process.
The group does not decide medical eligibility or receive confidential details. Use authorized roles.
This preserves the correct distinction and decision route without promising a particular outcome. Discuss the work facts and involve the coordinator appropriately.

lessons.transfer: Draft a practice private response acknowledging a request, describing the work question and identifying the proper next process without asking for medical documentation.

move.control: You can recognize and route the request promptly.
move.failure: A shared feature or general rule is used to bypass individual consideration.
move.next: Keep work facts, medical documentation and decision authority in their appropriate roles.

lessons.title: Check whether the work actually improved
lessons.summary: Attendance, installed features and completed tickets are different from effective participation and usable work.
lessons.objective: Distinguish implementation evidence from evidence of task effectiveness.
objectives: Distinguish implementation evidence from evidence of task effectiveness.
Plan a focused follow-up that respects confidentiality.
Identify a changed circumstance that needs renewed shared review or accommodation discussion.
takeaways: A feature being enabled does not prove it is effective.
Use task feedback without collecting unnecessary personal information.
Changed tools and circumstances can reopen a barrier.
lessons.statement: Follow-up asks whether people can now do the work, not simply whether the team completed an administrative step.

image.caption: A focused follow-up gives the owner evidence about what changed and what remains unresolved.

intro.heading: Check the result in the current setting
intro.body:
The DHS team improves its microphone setup, distributes a structured agenda and enables a caption feature. The project list says complete. At the next meeting, one speaker’s audio is still unclear and specialized program names are miscaptioned. The changes were implemented, but effectiveness remains partly unresolved. Ask about the relevant task and actual result instead of treating the installation or checkbox as a permanent pass.

Use a focused shared follow-up: could participants receive the information, enter the discussion, understand the decision and complete the next action? Record the specific barrier and responsible repair. A general satisfaction score can be useful in context but does not establish every person’s access or every technical requirement. A lack of complaints also does not prove that all barriers disappeared.

An approved individual accommodation has its own implementation and effectiveness questions through the policy. Installation, availability and usefulness are distinct. During delay, communicate through the appropriate process and consider feasible temporary assistance without promising an outcome beyond your role. Do not repeatedly collect medical proof yourself when a task fails; bring the unresolved work barrier to the coordinator and relevant support staff.

Changes may require renewed attention: a software update, new room, altered duty, revised document or different work arrangement can affect the result. Earlier success does not settle the current experience forever. Plan proportionate review using the responsible agency procedures and keep confidential records separate from broader team learning.

For the optional exercise, write a practice note with what was changed, what was actually checked, what remains uncertain and who will act next. Use non-identifying observations for shared improvement. The purpose is reliable follow-through across locations, not a ranking of employees by how easily they use a chosen method. A clearer process matters when it supports meaningful participation and the actual work result.

lessons.keyStatement: Implemented, available and effective are different claims; record the evidence for each.

flashcards.back: A change or arrangement was made. This shows action but does not by itself establish effective task access.
The relevant barrier is addressed in the current work situation. Use appropriate task evidence and the responsible process rather than assuming permanence.
A tool, room, duty or other condition has changed in a way that may affect access. It can require another appropriate review or exchange.
Using operational patterns to improve shared work without exposing a person’s medical history or confidential accommodation details.

items.title: Ask a concrete question
items.body: “Could you hear the room comments and follow the decision?” gives more usable information than “Was it fine?” Let people describe the actual task barrier without demanding that they identify the technical criterion or medical cause.

items.title: Keep the status honest
items.body: A tool installed or feature enabled is progress, not necessarily resolution. Name the result that has been verified and the part still pending. Assign the actual owner rather than shifting all review work to the participant who raised the issue.

items.title: Learn from a recurring barrier
items.body: Repeated failures may point toward a shared workflow issue, but investigate before claiming a cause. Repair templates, room setup or review routes where supported, and preserve the separate individual process when needed.

tabs.label: Attendance
tabs.body: Evidence of presence or connection, depending on the record. It does not by itself establish hearing, understanding, contribution or task completion.

tabs.label: Feature enabled
tabs.body: Evidence that a setting or tool was provided. Its accuracy, visibility and effectiveness in the task may still need review.

tabs.label: Task result
tabs.body: Evidence about the actual checked experience. Record the conditions and limits, and revisit meaningful changes rather than turning a past result into a permanent guarantee.

check.question: A caption feature is enabled, but important program terms are still wrong. What is the accurate status?
check.correct: The feature is enabled, but caption accuracy and effective access to the relevant information remain unresolved and need attention.
wrong: All access is complete because a feature exists.
The participant must be ungrateful for pointing out errors.
A new medical record must immediately be sent to the supervisor.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. This distinguishes the action taken from its result. The specific information problem can be reviewed without judging gratitude or improperly requesting medical documentation.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Enabling a feature does not prove that captions convey the required information accurately. A report of errors is not evidence that the participant is ungrateful; it identifies an effectiveness question. Supervisors and managers must not request accommodation medical information or documentation under Policy 1433, so an immediate medical record to the supervisor is not the response. Address the actual terms and errors through the responsible access process.

items.text: All participants signed into the call.
The approved meeting support was provided.
The tested task now permits the required input and correction.
The participant confirms the agreed support addresses the relevant current work barrier.
The new room’s audio has not been checked.
A software update changed the previously reviewed control.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to prepare and review a practice hybrid task. Related courses explain reasonable accommodation, digital standards and accessible procurement in more detail.

scenario.context: In this example, an employee’s approved tool worked until a software update changed the task. The supervisor says the old approval means the concern can be ignored.
options: Recognize the changed barrier, discuss the task result and involve the appropriate accommodation and technical processes while protecting confidentiality.
Close the concern because a past approval is permanent proof of effectiveness.
Publish the employee’s medical history in a shared issue log.
responses: This responds to the current situation and keeps the relevant roles distinct. The old decision informs the discussion but does not prove the new task works.
Changed conditions can affect effectiveness. A prior approval is not a reason to ignore the reported current barrier.
The issue log needs appropriate product and task information, not a medical history. Keep confidential records in the authorized process.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice follow-up with the action taken, checked result, remaining uncertainty and next owner. State which question belongs to shared work and which belongs to an individual process.

move.control: You can verify the actual task and preserve a route for further concerns.
move.failure: Attendance or an enabled feature becomes proof of lasting access.
move.next: Check the current work result, respond to changed barriers and report the status honestly.

jobAid.subtitle: Prepare, facilitate and follow through on accessible hybrid work
remember: Connection and attendance do not establish effective participation.
Usable shared practices help without replacing individual accommodation.
Ask about the task or service, not a diagnosis.
Use actual agency authority for telework, purchases and accommodation decisions.

sections.heading: Before the task
items: Map information, contribution and follow-up across room and remote settings.
Provide usable materials and a practical private request route.
Check the planned setup and services with appropriate support staff.

sections.heading: During and after
items: Identify speakers, support turn-taking and describe important visual meaning.
Connect remote contributions to the shared discussion and decision.
Respond appropriately when an access path fails.
Maintain usable documents, media and meaningful contribution routes.

sections.heading: Individual needs and follow-up
items: Recognize ordinary-language requests and forward them promptly through the policy.
Keep accommodation medical-documentation questions with the ADA Coordinator.
Separate shared repair from the individual decision and current support.
Distinguish implementation from effectiveness and revisit changed conditions.
